o1.biggest_strength: It targets the right segment and the pricing-change trigger, keeps every step link-free, and asks low-friction one-word questions that sound like one finance person talking to another. It also gives a clean reply and meeting forecast: about 7% replies and about 55 meetings across the 1,900.
o1.biggest_mistake: The 9-to-4-day proof is in step 1 and repeated in step 4, so the later steps have no new proof to add. It also leaves out practical send rules: no unsubscribe or footer, and no plan for handling replies.
o1.what_would_make_it_a_10: Move the proof out of step 1 into step 2. Add an opt-out footer and a short guide for handling replies. Add one timing insight tied to the finance calendar.

o2.biggest_strength: It reads like it was written by someone who knows finance. It times sends around month-end close and allows one contact per company. It adds an opt-out footer, a guide for handling replies, an A/B test and a clearly labelled bolder test, and all of it is grounded in the pilot numbers.
o2.biggest_mistake: Step 1 asks for a 20-minute walkthrough, and step 2 asks the Controller to bring in engineering for a call. Both are heavier asks than a cold first touch should make. The 12th–15th send window can also delay a fresh pricing trigger by weeks.
o2.what_would_make_it_a_10: Soften the step 1 and step 2 asks to simple replies. Let the send window flex so a trigger is never more than about two weeks old when step 1 goes out. Fix the fragment sentence in step 1.

reason: Both nail the segment, the trigger and the no-link rule. The second also understands our Controllers' calendar and gives me the operational pieces I'd need to run it, though its asks are a bit heavier than I'd like.
